newsitem.title: USA: Strong Ford results push up Sept. U.S. car sales.
newsitem.headline: Strong Ford results push up Sept. U.S. car sales.

text.p: Ford Motor Co.'s U.S. car and truck sales roared ahead in September with the help of aggressive pricing and incentives, lifting total industry light vehicle sales by a better-than-expected 5.7 percent margin from a year ago.

Ford, which claimed victory for its Taurus in the race for America's best selling car for the 1996 model year, reported that its car and light trucks sales rose 7.3 percent on a daily sales rate basis to 301,596 units from 292,695 a year ago. There were 24 selling days in September, compared with 25 in the same month of 1995.

"There must've been a very strong last week of the month," said Burnham Securities auto analyst David Healy, who noted that Ford, General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp. all performed better than indications early in the month.

Automakers reported total U.S. car and light truck of 1,207,100 units during September, up 5.7 percent from the 1,189,539 vehicles sold a year earlier. The seasonally adjusted annual sales rate for the month was 15 million units, even with a year ago but down from 15.8 million in August.

Analysts said, however, that the industry's September performance was actually much better than the annual rate suggests, because unusual seasonal adjustment factors supplied by the Commerce Department reduced the rate by 800,000 to 900,000 vehicles.
Chrysler on Tuesday reported a 21.9 percent gain in car and truck sales, while GM, reported a 2.7 percent decline, with lower car sales offsetting higher truck sales.
"Ford seems to be holding its own, and Chrysler seems to be taking market share away from GM," Healy said. "This will continue until GM gets more of its product lines replaced."

Ford's market share for the month rose to 25.01 percent from 24.6 percent a year earlier, While Chrysler's rose more than two percentage points to 15.23 percent. GM's meanwhile, dropped to 31 percent from 33.64 percent

Aided by a $1,500 incentive on its 1996 Taurus, Ford sold 45,204 of the mid-size sedans, up 53.1 percent from the 30,763 sold a year ago. The performance allowed Taurus to regain its calendar-year sales lead over its archrival, the Honda Accord.

For the 1996 model year ended Sept. 30, sales of the controversially styled Taurus fell 4.9 percent from a year ago to 378,144 cars, but were strong enough to best the 367,137 Accords and 354,035 Toyota Camrys sold during the period.
Ford's Lincoln luxury car sales, aided by a $37,950 one-price scheme for all three models, rose 40 percent from a year ago, while sales of Ford's F-Series pickup trucks rose 9.2 percent.
Robert Rewey, Ford's group vice president for marketing and sales, said he believed the outlook for the 1997 model year was healthy.

"Inflation appears to be in check, consumer confidence is high, the economy continues to grow moderately and interest rates have stayed in a range that historically has supported good sales levels," Rewey said in a statement.

Toyota Motor Corp. said its sales for September rose 14.2 percent to 85,091 vehicles, with domestic car sales up 11.3 percent and domestic truck sales up 47.8 percent. Improt car sales fell 7.2 percent, but import truck sales, led by the new 4Runner sport utility vehicle, rose 32.9 percent.

Honda Motor Co. Ltd. did not fare as well, reporting a 1 percent gain to 67,087 vehicles. Honda's domestic car sales rose 28.8 percent, but its imported car sales fell 7.2 percent and its truck sales were relatively flat.
Among other automakers reporting Thursday, Mercedes-Benz said its September U.S. sales rose 26 percent and Ford's Jaguar Cars Ltd. sales rose 25.8 percent.
For the first nine months of 1996, automakers sold a total of 11,637,108 light vehicles, up 2.8 percent from the same period of 1995.
